claim: Fluorescence microscopy is a fundamental tool in the life sciences.
source: Fluorescence microscopy is a fundamental tool in the life sciences, but the availability of sophisticated equipment required to yield high-quality, quantitative data is a major bottleneck in data production in many laboratories worldwide.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the introduction.

claim: The availability of sophisticated equipment required to yield high-quality, quantitative data is a major bottleneck in data production in many laboratories worldwide.
source: Fluorescence microscopy is a fundamental tool in the life sciences, but the availability of sophisticated equipment required to yield high-quality, quantitative data is a major bottleneck in data production in many laboratories worldwide.
evidence: This is presented as a known problem in the field.

claim: The abundancy of low-cost electronics and the simplification of fabrication through 3D-printing have led to the emergence of open-source scientific hardware as a research field.
source: This problem has long been recognized and the abundancy of low-cost electronics and the simplification of fabrication through 3D-printing have led to the emergence of open-source scientific hardware as a research field.
evidence: This is stated as a known development in the field.

claim: Cost effective fluorescence microscopes can be assembled from cheaply mass-produced components, but lag behind commercial solutions in image quality.
source: Cost effective fluorescence microscopes can be assembled from cheaply mass-produced components, but lag behind commercial solutions in image quality.

claim: The authors combined the UC2 microscopy toolbox with high-quality components and integrated electronics and software to assemble an automated high-resolution fluorescence microscope.

claim: The microscope demonstrates high resolution fluorescence imaging for fixed and live samples.

claim: When operated inside an incubator, long-term live-cell imaging over several days was possible.
source: When operated inside an incubator, long-term live-cell imaging over several days was possible.

claim: The microscope reaches single molecule sensitivity.
source: Our microscope reaches single molecule sensitivity, and we performed single particle tracking and SMLM super-resolution microscopy experiments in cells.

claim: The authors performed single particle tracking experiments in cells.
source: Our microscope reaches single molecule sensitivity, and we performed single particle tracking and SMLM super-resolution microscopy experiments in cells.

claim: The authors performed SMLM super-resolution microscopy experiments in cells.

claim: The setup costs a fraction of its commercially available counterparts but still provides a maximum of capabilities and image quality.
source: Our setup costs a fraction of its commercially available counterparts but still provides a maximum of capabilities and image quality.

claim: High quality scientific data can be generated by lay users with a low-budget system and open-source software.

evidence: This is supported by the experimental data demonstrating various imaging capabilities.

claim: The access to cutting-edge instrumentation is reserved to a subset of scientists as a result of its cost and technical complexity.

claim: The system is combined with a high NA objective, motorized stage and intuitive GUI-based operation.
source: Our system is based on the UC2 toolbox (Diederich et al., 2019a; Diederich et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022) using common optical elements, affordable electronic components and 3D printed parts and is combined with a high NA objective, motorized stage and intuitive GUI-based operation.

source: The result is a cost efficient and user-friendly high-resolution fluorescence microscope that is compatible with long-term live-cell imaging, single particle tracking and single molecule localization microscopy.

claim: All designs for the 3D parts, software and electronics are open-source.

claim: The quality of the objective is paramount to image quality.

source: We reasoned that the quality of the objective is paramount to image quality, while most other optical parts of a light microscope can be mass-produced components.

claim: A high-quality objective allows for the swift diagnosis of problems in the assembly of the optical path due to its high resolution and minimal chromatic and spatial aberrations.
source: Furthermore, such a high-quality objective allows for the swift diagnosis of problems in the assembly of the optical path due to its high resolution and minimal chromatic and spatial aberrations.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage based on optical principles.

claim: The authors decided to use an Olympus 1.49 NA oil objective.

claim: Any high-quality objective can be incorporated in the system by adapting the objective mount to the requirements of the objectives' manufacturer.

claim: The microscope is based on the UC2 toolbox using its injection molded cubes for the structural assembly.

evidence: This describes the structural basis of the microscope.

claim: The authors used an inverted configuration for ease of usage.

claim: The microscope was assembled in three layers to keep the size and design compact.

claim: The high-precision x-y sample table and z-stage were low-cost commercial solutions that were motorized and implemented into the open-source, python-based microscope GUI as automated elements of the microscope.

evidence: This describes the components used and is shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The emission pathway at the bottom of the microscope assembly is based on an Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera from Allied Vision.
source: The emission pathway at the bottom of the microscope assembly is based on an Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera from Allied Vision, which compared to conventional scientific cameras is more affordable by a factor of 30–60 times at the time of submission (Figure 1d), more compact and consumes less energy.
evidence: This describes the camera used and is shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera is more affordable than conventional scientific cameras by a factor of 30–60 times at the time of submission.
source: The emission pathway at the bottom of the microscope assembly is based on an Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera from Allied Vision, which compared to conventional scientific cameras is more affordable by a factor of 30–60 times at the time of submission (Figure 1d), more compact and consumes less energy.
evidence: This is a comparison of camera costs.

claim: The Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera is more compact than conventional scientific cameras.
source: The emission pathway at the bottom of the microscope assembly is based on an Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera from Allied Vision, which compared to conventional scientific cameras is more affordable by a factor of 30–60 times at the time of submission (Figure 1d), more compact and consumes less energy.
evidence: This is a comparison of camera characteristics.

claim: The Alvium 1800 U-158c CMOS camera consumes less energy than conventional scientific cameras.

evidence: This is a comparison of camera characteristics.

claim: The camera needs to be monochromatic as the Bayer pattern on a polychromatic camera would significantly reduce the sampling as well as the quantum efficiency of a camera chip.
source: One important point here is that the camera needs to be monochromatic as the Bayer pattern on a polychromatic camera would significantly reduce the sampling as well as the quantum efficiency of a camera chip, which is already lower compared to that of scientific cameras.
evidence: This is stated as a technical requirement based on optical principles.

claim: The quantum efficiency of the Alvium camera chip is already lower compared to that of scientific cameras.
source: One important point here is that the camera needs to be monochromatic as the Bayer pattern on a polychromatic camera would significantly reduce the sampling as well as the quantum efficiency of a camera chip, which is already lower compared to that of scientific cameras.
evidence: This is a comparison of camera characteristics.

claim: The camera was connected to the computer via USB 3.0, allowing fast data transfer and maximal compatibility.
source: The camera was connected to the computer via USB 3.0, allowing fast data transfer and maximal compatibility.
evidence: This describes the connection method used.

claim: The excitation pathway contained a low-cost 638 nm diode laser with an optional beam expander.
source: Between the emission pathway and the sample stage, the excitation pathway contained a low-cost 638 nm diode laser with an optional beam expander (Figure 1e), that depending on the illumination requirements could be inserted or removed, modulating the illumination density and homogeneity of the excitation field (see Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the excitation components and is shown in Figures 1e and 2c.

claim: The beam expander could be inserted or removed depending on the illumination requirements, modulating the illumination density and homogeneity of the excitation field.
source: Between the emission pathway and the sample stage, the excitation pathway contained a low-cost 638 nm diode laser with an optional beam expander (Figure 1e), that depending on the illumination requirements could be inserted or removed, modulating the illumination density and homogeneity of the excitation field (see Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the modularity of the excitation system and is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The authors used a low-cost Arduino-based board to trigger the laser, control laser power and to steer the x, y and z motors for focus and sample translation.
source: To trigger the laser, control laser power and to steer the x, y and z motors for focus and sample translation, we used a low-cost Arduino-based board that can be connected via USB3.0 to any computer.
evidence: This describes the control electronics used.

claim: Electronics on the board and the USB-camera are directly controlled via an adapted GUI of the python-based open-source software ImSwitch.
source: Electronics on the board and the USB-camera are then directly controlled via an adapted GUI of the python-based open-source software ImSwitch (Moreno et al., 2021), resulting in a fully automated microscope.
evidence: This describes the software control system and cites the ImSwitch software.

claim: ImSwitch includes the 'ImScript' an automation feature, which allows to execute a sequence of written Python commands with user defined parameters for example overnight time-series imaging experiments.
source: Additionally, ImSwitch includes the 'ImScript' an automation feature, which allows to execute a sequence of written Python commands with user defined parameters for example overnight time-series imaging experiments.
evidence: This describes a feature of the ImSwitch software.

claim: The authors implemented the recently presented OS SMLM algorithms microEye to realize an online-running localization framework that gives instant qualitative feedback if the sample preparation works as expected.
source: Furthermore, we took advantage of the open-source (OS) nature of ImSwitch and implemented the recently presented OS SMLM algorithms microEye (Alsamsam et al., 2022) to realize an online-running localization framework that gives instant qualitative feedback if the sample preparation works as expected.
evidence: This describes the implementation of microEye algorithms and cites the source.

claim: The feedback of online-running image processing algorithms can be looped back into the hardware control to eventually compensate possible drift (e.g. autofocus).
source: In addition, the feedback of these online-running image processing algorithms can be looped back into the hardware control to eventually compensate possible drift (e.g. autofocus).
evidence: This describes a capability of the system.

claim: A large variety of available Napari plugins can be used to directly work on the data without moving them to a different computer.
source: A large variety of available Napari (Damm et al., 2023) plugins can be used to directly work on the data without moving them to a different computer.
evidence: This describes a capability of the system and cites Napari.

claim: The low-cost laser had minor bands in the wavelength range of 650–670 nm.
source: Spectrometric measurement of the excitation laser beam confirmed that our low-cost laser had minor bands in the wavelength range of 650–670 nm, which we could remove using an additional band pass excitation filter (ZET635/20 X).
evidence: This is supported by spectrometric measurement data.

claim: The minor bands in the wavelength range of 650–670 nm could be removed using an additional band pass excitation filter (ZET635/20 X).
source: Spectrometric measurement of the excitation laser beam confirmed that our low-cost laser had minor bands in the wavelength range of 650–670 nm, which we could remove using an additional band pass excitation filter (ZET635/20 X).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The authors motorized an x-y stage via torque transmission from the motor to the micrometer screws of the stage via timing belts.
source: To render all three axes of movement computer controlled, we first motorized an x-y stage via torque transmission form the motor to the micrometer screws of the stage via timing belts.
evidence: This describes the motorization method used.

claim: The authors incorporated a motorized lead screw-driven z-stage holding the objective into the modular design of the microscope.
source: Secondly, we incorporated a motorized lead screw-driven (NEMA11, 50 mm, Amazon, 50€) z-stage holding the objective into the modular design of the microscope.
evidence: This describes the z-stage component used.

claim: When the authors imaged fixed mammalian cells stained against tubulin via immunofluorescence using AF647 with moderate laser intensity (35 W/cm2), beam expander and 50ms integration time, cells were evenly illuminated.
source: When we imaged these cells with moderate laser intensity (35 W/cm2), beam expander and 50ms integration time, we found that cells were evenly illuminated (Figure 2a) and microtubules appeared as diffraction-limited lines inside cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Microtubules appeared as diffraction-limited lines inside cells when imaged with moderate laser intensity (35 W/cm2), beam expander and 50ms integration time.
source: When we imaged these cells with moderate laser intensity (35 W/cm2), beam expander and 50ms integration time, we found that cells were evenly illuminated (Figure 2a) and microtubules appeared as diffraction-limited lines inside cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by the image data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The measured fluorescence intensity was quite homogenous across the field of view, with variations of up to 25% of the maximal fluorescence intensity, excluding the bottom left and right corners.
source: The measured fluorescence intensity was quite homogenous across the field of view, with variations of up to 25% of the maximal fluorescence intensity, excluding the bottom left and right corners (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the illumination profile data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The authors consistently found drift of less than 1 µm over 2 hr when imaging sub-diffraction fluorescent beads repeatedly over time.
source: When we then calculated the displacement of the beads over time, we consistently found drift of less than 1 µm over 2 hr (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the bead tracking data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The microscope is suitable for imaging experiments that require repeated measurements of the same field of view such as live-cell imaging.
source: We concluded that our microscope may be suitable for imaging experiments that require repeated measurements of the same field of view such as live-cell imaging.
evidence: This is inferred from the low drift measurements.

claim: Cells tolerated acquisition conditions for several hours without damage visible in fluorescence or widefield image when repeatedly illuminated with moderate laser power (18 W/cm2) to excite SiR-actin fluorescence and with white light in transmission mode.
source: When we then repeatedly illuminated the cells with moderate laser power (18 W/cm2) to excite SiR-actin fluorescence and with white light in transmission mode to image the cells, we found that the cells tolerated acquisition conditions for several hours without damage visible in fluorescence or widefield image (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Drift was negligible during live-cell imaging at room temperature.
source: As expected, drift was negligible.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the live-cell imaging experiment.

claim: The authors found similar stability against drift over time when the experiment was performed not on an optical table, but a wetlab bench over a layer of foam material.
source: Importantly, we found similar stability against drift over time, when we performed this experiment not on an optical table, but a wetlab bench over a layer of foam material (made of Polyethylene or alternatively Polyurethane) as a damping layer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different setups.

claim: The microscope might be suitable for long-term imaging in an environment that does not provide vibration damping, such as a cell culture incubator.
source: This suggested that our microscope might be suitable for long-term imaging in an environment that does not provide vibration damping, such as a cell culture incubator.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability measurements on a wetlab bench.

claim: The microscope assembly is of small size and connected via two flexible USB cables.
source: Given that our microscope assembly is of small size, and connected via two flexible USB cables, we then moved on to perform live-cell imaging over longer periods in a cell culture incubator.
evidence: This describes the physical characteristics of the microscope.

claim: T98G cancer cells exhibited normal morphology and growth over many hours when plated on coverslips and mounted on the microscope sample holder in warm medium inside the incubator.
source: When we plated live T98G cancer cells on coverslips and mounted them on the microscope sample holder in warm medium inside the incubator, they exhibited normal morphology and growth over many hours.
evidence: This is supported by observation of cell behavior.

claim: Cells kept dividing and moving on the coverslip for several days during long-term imaging using Syto deep-red fluorescence staining of the nucleus.
source: When we performed a long-term imaging experiment using Syto deep-red fluorescence staining of the nucleus (Thermo Fisher), we found that cells kept dividing and moving on the coverslip for several days (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the long-term imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The setup was compatible with long-term live-cell imaging of cells.
source: We concluded that our setup was compatible with long-term live-cell imaging of cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the long-term imaging experiments.

claim: The authors detected QDs readily as single diffraction limited entities on cells when CV-1 cells stably expressing GPI-GFP were incubated with streptavidin 655 nm quantum dots coupled to biotin-tagged anti-GFP nanobodies.
source: When we incubated these cells with streptavidin 655 nm quantum dots (QDs) coupled to biotin-tagged anti-GFP nanobodies (Figure 5a), we detected QDs readily as single diffraction limited entities on cells (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by the single particle imaging data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The authors could generate trajectories over many frames when they localized emission centers and tracked the QDs over time.
source: When we then localized emission centers and tracked the QDs over time, we could generate trajectories over many frames (Figure 5c and d) and extract parameters describing particle movement such as the diffusion coefficient (D, Figure 5e) and the moment scaling spectrum (MSS, Figure 5f; Ewers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the tracking data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: The authors extracted parameters describing particle movement such as the diffusion coefficient and the moment scaling spectrum.
source: When we then localized emission centers and tracked the QDs over time, we could generate trajectories over many frames (Figure 5c and d) and extract parameters describing particle movement such as the diffusion coefficient (D, Figure 5e) and the moment scaling spectrum (MSS, Figure 5f; Ewers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figures 5e and 5f.

claim: The MSS introduces a parameter that allows to quantitatively describe the type of motion a particle undergoes (MSS = 0 being immobility,<0.5 Brownian diffusion and >0.5 super-diffusive).
source: The MSS introduces a parameter that allows to quantitatively describe the type of motion a particle undergoes (MSS = 0 being immobility,<0.5 Brownian diffusion and >0.5 super-diffusive).
evidence: This is stated as a definition of the MSS parameter.

claim: The measurements were in agreement with previous observations by the authors.
source: Our measurements were in agreement with our previous observations (Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The intense staining quickly faded and gave way to the typically observed blinking in SMLM experiments when the sample was illuminated with high intensity laser light (~1kW/cm2).
source: When we then illuminated our sample with high intensity laser light (in our case ~1kW/cm2), we found that the intense staining quickly faded and gave way to the typically observed blinking in SMLM experiments.
evidence: This is supported by observation during SMLM experiments.

claim: The authors achieved a drastic improvement in resolution in reconstructed SMLM micrographs even though they were limited to widefield illumination.
source: Even though we were limited to widefield illumination, we achieved a drastic improvement in resolution in reconstructed SMLM micrographs (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of widefield and SMLM images in Figure 6a.

claim: The authors could easily detect the typical 'railroad track' pattern with a spacing of 38–43 nm when they measured the profile of individual microtubules, indicative of high-quality SMLM imaging.
source: When we measured the profile of individual microtubules, we could easily detect the typical 'railroad track' pattern with a spacing of 38–43 nm, indicative of high-quality SMLM imaging (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is supported by the profile measurements shown in Figures 6b and 6c.

claim: The overall achieved resolution was 93 nm, clearly below the optical resolution limit.
source: To quantify the achieved resolution, we used Fourier ring correlation (Nieuwenhuizen et al., 2013) and found that the overall achieved resolution was 93 nm, clearly below the optical resolution limit (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by the Fourier ring correlation analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The authors developed a cost effective, high-quality automated microscope that can be assembled by laypeople with minimal background knowledge in optics, electronics and informatics.
source: Here, we developed a cost effective, high-quality automated microscope that can be assembled by laypeople with minimal background knowledge in optics, electronics and informatics.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript supported by the assembly instructions and experimental data.

claim: The assembly guidelines including CAD files of the 3D printed parts, list of used components and software are openly accessible on the Github repositories.
source: The assembly guidelines including CAD files of the 3D printed parts, list of used components and software are openly accessible on the Github repositories (see Table 1), thus offering maximal availability.
